(np.arange(NBINS) + 1)\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# ONE access\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n_ONE = None\n_BRAIN_REGIONS = None\n\n\ndef get_one():\n    \"\"\"Build (once per process) a ONE client against the staged local cache.\n\n    The default (remote) mode is used deliberately: it resolves datasets through the\n    cached Alyx REST responses in `<cache>/.rest`, which know about the dataset revisions\n    that are actually staged on disk (e.g. `alf/#2025-03-03#/_ibl_trials.table.pqt`).\n    The copied `Brainwidemap` release table predates those revisions, so `mode='local'`\n    silently fails to find the trials table.\n    \"\"\"\n    global _ONE\n    if _ONE is None:\n        _ONE = ONE(base_url=ONE_BASE_URL, silent=True, cache_dir=ONE_CACHE_DIR)\n    return _ONE\n\n\ndef get_brain_regions():\n    global _BRAIN_REGIONS\n    if _BRAIN_REGIONS is None:\n        _BRAIN_REGIONS = BrainRegions()\n    return _BRAIN_REGIONS\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Neural data\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\ndef load_session_spikes(one, eid, pids, pnames):\n    \"\"\"Load and merge the spike sorting of every probe of a session.\n\n    Mirrors `ibl_data_utils.prepare_data`: each probe is loaded with\n    `SpikeSortingLoader.load_spike_sorting` + `merge_clusters`, then probes are merged with\n    the reference `merge_probes` helper (neurons of one session are pooled across probes\n    because the probes are not statistically independent -- see the data paper,\n    \"Overview of decoding\").\n\n    The reference additionally queries `raw_electrophysiology(band='ap', stream=True).fs`\n    to record the AP sampling rate. That streams raw ephys over the network and is not\n    used by any downstream computation, so it is skipped.\n    \"\"\"\n    spikes_list, clusters_list = [], []\n    for pid, pname in zip(pids, pnames):\n        ssl = SpikeSortingLoader(pid=str(pid), one=one, eid=eid, pname=pname)\n        sp, cl, ch = ssl.load_spike_sorting()\n        if sp is None or 'times' not in sp or len(sp['times']) == 0:\n            continue\n        if cl is None or len(cl.get('channels', [])) == 0:\n            continue\n        cld = SpikeSortingLoader.merge_clusters(sp, cl, ch).to_df()\n        cld['pid'] = str(pid)\n        spikes_list.append(sp)\n        clusters_list.append(cld)\n    if not spikes_list:\n        raise RuntimeError('no spike sorting could be loaded for this session')\n    return merge_probes(spikes_list, clusters_list)\n\n\ndef select_neurons(clusters, brain_regions):\n    \"\"\"Apply the data paper's neuron and region inclusion criteria.\n\n    * `label >= 1` keeps only \"well-isolated neurons\": in `ibllib`, `label` is the fraction\n      of the three RIGOR single-unit metrics a cluster passes (amplitude > 50 uV,\n      noise cut-off < 20 uV, refractory-period violation), so `label == 1` is exactly the\n      data paper's criterion.\n    * Beryl acronyms `root` / `void` are dropped, implementing the data paper's restriction\n      to regions \"designated grey matter in the adult mouse Allen CCF\". The reference code\n      makes the same exclusion in `MultiRegionDataModule.list_regions`.\n\n    Returns (keep_idx, beryl_acronyms_of_kept_neurons).\n    \"\"\"\n    beryl = np.asarray(brain_regions.acronym2acronym(\n        clusters['acronym'].to_numpy(), mapping='Beryl'))\n    good = clusters['label'].to_numpy() >= QC_LABEL\n    grey = ~np.isin(beryl, NON_GREY_MATTER)\n    keep = np.nonzero(good & grey)[0]\n    return keep, beryl[keep]\n\n\ndef bin_spiking_data_fast(spike_times, spike_clusters, n_clusters, align_times):\n    \"\"\"Bin spikes into (n_trials, n_clusters, NBINS) counts.\n\n    Vectorised equivalent of the reference `bin_spiking_data` /\n    `get_spike_data_per_interval`, which calls `iblutil.numerical.bincount2D` once per\n    trial inside a multiprocessing pool. `bincount2D` assigns a sample to bin\n    `floor((t - t_beg) / binsize)` over `[t_beg, t_end]` and the reference then truncates\n    to the first `NBINS` columns, so a spike landing exactly on `t_end` is dropped. The\n    same convention is reproduced here (spikes are taken from `[t_beg, t_end)` and bin\n    indices outside `[0, NBINS)` are discarded).\n\n    Args:\n        spike_times: (n_spikes,) spike times, sorted ascending.\n        spike_clusters: (n_spikes,) cluster index in `[0, n_clusters)`.\n        n_clusters: number of neurons.\n        align_times: (n_trials,) alignment event times.\n\n    Returns:\n        (n_trials, n_clusters, NBINS) uint8 array of spike counts.\n    \"\"\"\n    beg = align_times + TIME_WINDOW[0]\n    end = align_times + TIME_WINDOW[1]\n    out = np.zeros((len(align_times), n_clusters, NBINS), dtype=np.uint8)\n    finite = np.isfinite(beg) & np.isfinite(end)\n    i0 = np.searchsorted(spike_times, np.where(finite, beg, np.inf), side='left')\n    i1 = np.searchsorted(spike_times, np.where(finite, end, np.inf), side='left')\n    for k in range(len(align_times)):\n        if not finite[k]:\n            continue\n        t = spike_times[i0[k]:i1[k]]\n        c = spike_clusters[i0[k]:i1[k]]\n        b = np.floor((t - beg[k]) / BINSIZE).astype(np.int64)\n        ok = (b >= 0) & (b < NBINS)\n        counts = np.bincount(c[ok] * NBINS + b[ok], minlength=n_clusters * NBINS)\n        np.clip(counts, 0, 255, out=counts)\n        out[k] = counts.reshape(n_clusters, NBINS).astype(np.uint8)\n    return out\n\n\ndef neural_data_available(all_spike_times, align_times):\n    \"\"\"Mask of trials whose 2 s window is covered by valid electrophysiology.\n\n    Neither the data paper nor the reference code names a criterion for this, but real\n    sessions contain periods with no neural data at all: some recordings stop while the\n    behavioural rig keeps running (e.g. eid 8c2f7f4d…: last spike at 1779 s, three more\n    trials afterwards), and some spike trains contain multi-second dropouts (e.g. eid\n    b182b754…: a 5 s hole at 185-190 s). Those trials are all-zero and carry no\n    information, and `verify_data_format` flags them.\n\n    Detection uses the *pooled, unfiltered* spike train of the session (all Kilosort\n    clusters of all probes, ~900 per probe firing at a combined rate of thousands of\n    spikes per second), so any inter-spike interval longer than `MAX_SPIKE_GAP` = 0.5 s\n    is unambiguously missing data rather than silence. A trial is rejected if its window\n    intersects such a gap, or starts before the first / ends after the last spike.\n\n    Args:\n        all_spike_times: (n,) pooled spike times of every cluster, sorted ascending.\n        align_times: (n_trials,) alignment event times.\n\n    Returns:\n        (n_trials,) bool mask, True where neural data covers the whole window.\n    \"\"\"\n    beg = align_times + TIME_WINDOW[0]\n    end = align_times + TIME_WINDOW[1]\n    ok = np.isfinite(beg) & np.isfinite(end)\n    if len(all_spike_times) == 0:\n        return np.zeros(len(align_times), dtype=bool)\n\n    # no-data intervals: before the first spike, after the last, and every long ISI\n    dt = np.diff(all_spike_times)\n    idx = np.nonzero(dt > MAX_SPIKE_GAP)[0]\n    gap_start = np.concatenate([[-np.inf], all_spike_times[idx], [all_spike_times[-1]]])\n    gap_end = np.concatenate([[all_spike_times[0]], all_spike_times[idx + 1], [np.inf]])\n\n    # a trial is bad if [beg, end) overlaps any [gap_start, gap_end]\n    safe_beg = np.where(ok, beg, 0.0)\n    safe_end = np.where(ok, end, 0.0)\n    overlaps = (safe_beg[:, None] < gap_end[None, :]) & (safe_end[:, None] > gap_start[None, :])\n    return ok & ~overlaps.any(axis=1)\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# Behaviour\n# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------\ndef load_dynamic_behaviour(sess_loader):\n    \"\"\"Load the two time-varying behaviours the decoder has to predict.\n\n    Reproduces `ibl_data_utils.load_target_behavior`:\n      * wheel speed  = |velocity| of the uniformly resampled (~1 kHz) wheel trace,\n      * whisker motion energy = `whiskerMotionEnergy` of the **left** camera (60 Hz),\n        falling back to the right camera (150 Hz) when the left one is unavailable --\n        exactly the fallback in `ibl_data_utils.bin_behaviors`.\n\n    Returns {'wheel-speed': (times, values), 'whisker-motion-energy': (times, values)},\n    plus the camera actually used.\n    \"\"\"\n    out = {}\n    sess_loader.load_wheel()\n    out['wheel-speed'] = (sess_loader.wheel['times'].to_numpy(),\n                          np.abs(sess_loader.wheel['velocity'].to_numpy()))\n\n    camera_used = None\n    for view, key in (('left', 'leftCamera'), ('right', 'rightCamera')):\n        try:\n            sess_loader.load_motion_energy(views=[view])\n            me = sess_loader.motion_energy[key]\n            times = me['times'].to_numpy()\n            vals = me['whiskerMotionEnergy'].to_numpy()\n            if len(times) == 0 or np.all(np.isnan(vals)):\n                continue\n            out['whisker-motion-energy'] = (times, vals)\n            camera_used = view\n            break\n        except Exception:\n            continue\n    if camera_used is None:\n        raise RuntimeError('no whisker motion energy available')\n    return out, camera_used\n\n\ndef bin_behaviour_per_trial(target_times, target_vals, align_times):\n    \"\"\"Resample a behavioural trace onto the 100 trial bins, per trial.\n\n    Faithful re-implementation of `ibl_data_utils.get_behavior_per_interval`:\n      * the trace is sliced to the open interval (t_beg, t_end),\n      * a trial is rejected when there is no data, when the trace starts more than one bin\n        after `t_beg` or ends more than one bin before `t_end`, when the interval time is\n        NaN, or when the slice contains NaNs,\n      * the remaining trials are linearly interpolated (with linear extrapolation at the\n        edges) onto `np.linspace(t_beg + binsize, t_end, n_bins)`, i.e. the right edge of\n        each bin.\n\n    The only deviation is that NaNs always reject a trial (the reference's\n    `allow_nans=False` branch). loads each probe with `load_spiking_data`; `merge_probes`; `load_trials_and_mask(max_trial_len=10.0)`; `load_anytime_behaviors` |\n| `load_spiking_data` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | LOADING/CURATION | `SpikeSortingLoader.load_spike_sorting()` + `merge_clusters(...).to_df()`. `qc=None` (default) keeps every cluster; `qc=1` keeps `label >= 1` (\"good\"/well-isolated) |\n| `merge_probes` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | LOADING | concatenates probes of one session into a single cluster/spike set, re-indexing `spikes['clusters']`, re-sorting spikes by time |\n| `load_trials_and_mask` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | CURATION | `SessionLoader.load_trials()`; builds a boolean mask excluding RT<0.08 s, RT>2 s, `feedback_times-goCue_times > max_trial_len`, NaN in {stimOn_times, choice, feedback_times, probabilityLeft, firstMovement_times, feedbackType}, and `choice == 0` |\n| `list_brain_regions` / `select_brain_regions` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | PROCESSING | `BrainRegions().acronym2acronym(..., mapping='Beryl')`; with `single_region=False` returns one group with **all** Beryl regions |\n| `bin_spiking_data` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | PROCESSING | intervals = `stimOn_times + (-0.5, 1.5)`; per-trial `bincount2D(times, clusters, xbin=0.02, xlim=[t_beg,t_end])`, truncated to `n_bins = ceil(2/0.02) = 100` |\n| `get_spike_data_per_interval` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | PROCESSING | the per-trial worker for the above (multiprocessing) |\n| `load_target_behavior` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | LOADING | `SessionLoader.load_wheel()` → `wheel-speed = abs(velocity)`; `SessionLoader.load_motion_energy(views=['left'/'right'])` → `whiskerMotionEnergy` |\n| `get_behavior_per_interval` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | PROCESSING | slices the behavioural trace to the trial interval and `interp1d`-resamples onto `np.linspace(beg+binsize, end, n_bins)` (i.e. the **right edge of each 20 ms bin**); marks the interval bad if the trace starts >1 bin late or ends >1 bin early, if the interval time is NaN, or (when `allow_nans=False`) if it contains NaNs |\n| `bin_behaviors` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | PROCESSING | builds `choice`, `block` (=`probabilityLeft`), `reward` (=`rewardVolume>1`), `contrast` per trial, plus the interpolated dynamic traces; called with `allow_nans=True` |\n| `align_spike_behavior` | `src/utils/ibl_data_utils.py` | CURATION | drops trials where any behaviour is `None` **and** trials failing `trials_mask` |\n| `standardize_spike_data` | `src/utils/data_loader_utils.py` | PROCESSING | per-time-bin z-scoring; belongs to the *model*, not the dataset (their cached HF dataset stores raw spike counts as `np.ubyte`) |\n\n### Notes\n- The cached dataset the reference writes contains **raw spike counts** per (trial, time-bin,\n  neuron), stored sparsely as unsigned bytes. Standardisation happens at model-fit time.\n  Our target format wants neural activity per trial as `(n_neurons, n_timepoints)`, so we\n  store the same raw spike counts (as `float32`), transposed.\n- `prepare_data` calls `load_spiking_data` **without** `qc`, i.e. it keeps all Kilosort\n  clusters including MUA. The data paper instead uses only well-isolated neurons\n  (`label >= 1`). See Step 4 for how this discrepancy is resolved.\n- `load_spiking_data` also calls `spike_loader.raw_electrophysiology(band=\"ap\", stream=True).fs`\n  purely to record the AP sampling rate in metadata. That streams raw data over the network\n  and is not needed for binning, so it is not reproduced here.\n- The decoding scripts (`1_/2_/3_decode_*.py`, `utils/data_loader_utils.py`) show how the\n  cached data is consumed: `choice` as a classification target, `wheel-speed` /\n  `whisker-motion-energy` as **time-varying** (length-T) regression targets, `block`/prior\n  per trial. `MultiRegionDataModule.list_regions` excludes `root` and `void`.\n\n---\n\n## Step 2: Dataset Exploration\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Data Structure\n`/app/data/one_cache/` is a standard ONE reference code `params` |\n| Behaviour sampling | 60 Hz (left camera), wheel ~1 kHz | methodpaper: \"wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time-varying signals sampled at 60 Hz\" |\n\n### Processing Details\n- **Temporal alignment**: `stimOn_times`, window `(-0.5, +1.5)` s, 20 ms bins → T = 100.\n  (The STAR-Methods prose mentions 50-ms bins for the choice/prior *decoders*; the released\n  caching code and the model description both use 20 ms / T = 100, and the task here needs\n  time-resolved behaviour, so 20 ms is used. See Step 4.)\n- **Neural**: raw spike counts per bin, all neurons of a session pooled across probes.\n- **Behaviour**: wheel speed = `|velocity|` of the ~1 kHz resampled wheel; whisker motion\n  energy from the left camera (right camera as fallback); both linearly interpolated onto\n  the right edge of each 20 ms bin.\n\n### Curation Steps\n\n**Neuron curation rules** (datapaper): exclude units failing any RIGOR single-unit metric —\namplitude > 50 µV, noise cut-off < 20 µV, refractory-period violation. Survivors are\n\"well-isolated neurons\" (621,733 → 75,708). In `ibllib` this is exactly the\n`clusters['label'] >= 1` flag produced by `SpikeSortingLoader.merge_clusters`.\nAnalyses further restrict to **grey-matter** regions.\n\n**Trial curation rules** (datapaper, and `load_trials_and_mask` in the reference code):\nexclude a trial if any of `choice, probabilityLeft, feedbackType, feedback_times,\nstimOn_times, firstMovement_times` is undetected (NaN), or if\n`firstMovement_times − stimOn_times ∉ [0.08, 2.00] s`. The reference code additionally\ndrops `choice == 0` (no response) and trials with `feedback_times − goCue_times > 10 s`.\n\n**Session curation**: release-level criteria (≥250 trials, ≥90% correct on 100% contrast,\n≥3 error trials, hardware QC, resolved histology) are already applied to the 459 released\nsessions. The method paper ends up with 433 sessions, i.e. ~26 are lost, consistent with\nmissing/unusable video (whisker motion energy) data.\n\n### Decoders Trained (values reported in the reference papers)\n| Decoded variable | Metric | Reported value |\n|---|---|---|\n| Choice (region-level, method paper Fig. 4/5) | AUC | ~0.66 (linear) → 0.72 (RRR) → 0.79 (combined), example session |\n| Prior | Pearson r | 0.05 (single-session) → 0.34 / 0.65 (multi-session / oracle) |\n| Wheel speed | R² | 0.24 (linear) → 0.49–0.55 (RRR) |\n| Whisker motion energy | R² | 0.52–0.55 → 0.75–0.80 |\n| Choice/stimulus/feedback (data paper) | balanced accuracy | region-level effect sizes, small (a few % above 0.5) for most regions |\n\nThese are *region-level, single-session* numbers, so they are a lower bound for what a\nwhole-session decoder should achieve; they are not directly comparable to the\nper-timepoint balanced accuracies produced by `/app/train_decoder.py`.\n\n---\n\n## Step 4: Check for Consistency\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Discrepancies Found\n| Topic | Reference code says | Data shows | Papers say | Resolution |\n|-------|--------------------|------------|------------|------------|\n| Time bin for choice/prior decoding | `binsize = 0.02` in `0_data_caching.py` | n/a | methodpaper STAR Methods prose: \"50-ms non-overlapping time bins\" for choice/prior; the 50 ms sentence describes a separate per-trial decoding experiment. 20 ms is also required here because wheel speed and whisker motion energy must be decoded *per timepoint*, and the reference itself uses 20 ms for those. |\n| Alignment event | `align_time = 'stimOn_times'`, window `(-0.5, 1.5)` | `trials.stimOn_times` present in all sessions | choice aligned to stimulus onset −0.5…+1.5 s; (b) the method paper's phrase \"all neurons\" contrasts with its *region-restricted* decoders, not with QC; (c) including all 621k multi-unit clusters would make the converted dataset ~10x larger (≈120 GB) for units that the data paper explicitly says are not separable neurons. Documented as a deliberate departure from `0_data_caching.py`. |\n| Grey matter | `list_brain_regions` keeps every Beryl acronym incl. `root`/`void`; but `MultiRegionDataModule.list_regions` drops `root` and `void` | ~15% of good clusters map to `root`/`void` | datapaper: \"restricted to regions that were designated grey matter in the adult mouse Allen CCF\" | **Drop `root`/`void`.** Consistent with the data paper and with the reference code's own region listing. |\n| Trial exclusion | `load_trials_and_mask(one, eid, max_trial_len=10.0)` → RT ∈ [0.08, 2] s, no NaN in 6 events, `choice != 0`, `feedback_times − goCue_times <= 10 s` | 34% of raw trials excluded | datapaper lists exactly the 6 NaN events and the 0.08–2.00 s reaction-time window; 22.8% of trials have RT < 80 ms | **Use `load_trials_and_mask` verbatim** (imported from the reference module), including `max_trial_len=10.0`, which is the reference code's only addition. |\n| `SessionLoader` call signature | reference calls `SessionLoader(one, eid)` positionally | ibllib 4.0.1 `SessionLoader` is a keyword-only dataclass | — | Pass an explicit `sess_loader=SessionLoader(one=one, eid=eid)` into `load_trials_and_mask`. Pure API adaptation, no change in behaviour. |\n| AP sampling frequency | `load_spiking_data` calls `raw_electrophysiology(band='ap', stream=True).fs` | requires streaming raw ephys from the network | — | Skipped: it only fills a metadata field and is never used downstream. |\n| NaNs in behaviour | `bin_behaviors(..., allow_nans=True)`; the model later imputes NaNs with the trial average | NaNs do occur in whisker ME and (rarely) wheel | — | Use the reference's `allow_nans=False` branch (reject the trial). The converted outputs are class labels, so there is no sensible \"NaN class\", and `verify_data_format` errors on NaNs. |\n| ONE cache access | reference builds `ONE(..., password='international', cache_dir=...)` (auto mode) | `mode='local'` + `load_cache(tag='Brainwidemap')` cannot see the staged dataset revisions | — | Default (remote) mode against the staged `.rest` response cache and auth token; verified to return all 20 trial columns (Step 0). |\n| Session list | reference reads `data/bwm_release.csv` (the BWM freeze file) | 459 eids / 699 pids / 139 subjects on disk | datapaper: 459 sessions, 699 insertions, 139 mice | **Use `bwm_release.csv`**, exactly as the reference does. |\n\nAfter these resolutions the three sources agree: same session list, same trial mask, same\nalignment/binning, same behavioural signals; the only substantive addition is the data\npaper's neuron QC + grey-matter restriction, which the method-paper code omits.\n\n---\n\n## Step 5: Mapping Planning\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Variable Mapping\n| Source (ONE object.attribute) | Target field | Transform | Reference code function(s) | Notes |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| `spikes.times`, `spikes.clusters` (all probes) + `clusters.label`, `clusters.acronym` | `neural[session][trial]` (n_neurons, 100) float32 | pool probes → keep `label>=1` & Beryl ∉ {root, void} → count spikes in 100 × 20 ms bins over `stimOn_times + (-0.5, 1.5)` | `prepare_data`, `load_spiking_data`, `merge_probes`, `list_brain_regions`, `select_brain_regions`, `bin_spiking_data` | spike **counts**, not rates, matching the reference cached dataset |\n| bin index | `input[…][0]` | signed bin-centre time, −0.49 … +1.49 s | — (task spec: \"time since stimulus onset, continuous, time-varying\") | constant grid, identical for every trial |\n| `trials.probabilityLeft` | `input[…][1]` | 0-based index of the trial within its run of constant `probabilityLeft`, computed on the **unfiltered** trials table, broadcast over the 100 bins | — (task spec: \"trial number in block, continuous, per-trial\") | block structure must come from all trials, not the filtered subset |\n| `trials.choice` | `output[…][0]` | `+1 → 0` (left), `−1 → 1` (right); `0` (no response) already excluded | `bin_behaviors` (`choice`) | direction verified empirically, see sanity checks |\n| `trials.probabilityLeft` | `output[…][1]` | `0.2 → 0`, `0.5 → 1`, `0.8 → 2` | `bin_behaviors` (`block`) | exactly as required by the task spec |\n| `wheel.velocity` (SessionLoader, ~1 kHz resampled) | `output[…][2]` | `abs(velocity)` → interpolate onto the right edge of each 20 ms bin → per-session tertiles → {0,1,2} | `load_target_behavior('wheel-speed')`, `get_behavior_per_interval` | time-varying |\n| `leftCamera.ROIMotionEnergy` (`whiskerMotionEnergy`, 60 Hz; right camera fallback) | `output[…][3]` | interpolate onto bin right edges → per-session tertiles → {0,1,2} | `load_target_behavior('left-whisker-motion-energy')`, fallback logic in `bin_behaviors` | time-varying |\n| `clusters.acronym` → Beryl | `brain_regions`, `brain_region_idx` | `BrainRegions().acronym2acronym(..., mapping='Beryl')` | `list_brain_regions` | |\n| `bwm_release.csv` `subject` | `subjects`, `subject_idx` | unique sorted subject names | `0_data_caching.py` | |\n\n### Key Decisions\n1. **Alignment = `stimOn_times`, window (−0.5, +1.5) s, 20 ms bins (T = 100).** Exactly the\n   reference `params`; also what the task specification requires.\n2. **Spike counts, unnormalised.** The reference caches raw counts (`np.ubyte`) and\n   z-scores only inside the model (`standardize_spike_data`). `train_decoder.py` does its\n   own SVD-based projection, so raw counts are the right thing to store.\n3. **Neuron QC: `label >= 1` + grey matter.** See Step 4. Sanity check: this must give\n   ≈108 neurons per probe and ≈62–63k neurons in total.\n4. **Trial QC: reference `load_trials_and_mask(max_trial_len=10.0)`**, imported directly\n   from the reference module so the logic cannot drift.\n5. **Behaviour-coverage QC.** A trial is dropped when the wheel or whisker trace does not\n   cover the whole 2 s window (the reference's \"target data starts too late / ends too\n   early\" tests) or contains NaN.\n6. **Ephys-coverage QC (addition).** A trial is dropped when its window intersects a\n   >0.5 s gap in the *pooled unfiltered* spike train or falls outside the recorded\n   interval. Necessary because some sessions keep running the behavioural rig after the\n   ephys stops; those trials would otherwise be all-zero.\n7. **Session QC: ≥5 well-isolated grey-matter neurons** (the data paper's per-session\n   neuron minimum), a usable whisker trace, and ≥2 usable trials.\n8. **Per-session tertiles for the two continuous outputs.** Both signals are in\n   session-specific units (motion energy is an uncalibrated pixel difference that depends\n   on camera resolution/frame rate, illumination and ROI placement; wheel speed depends on\n   how vigorously the individual mouse turns). Per-session tertiles make chance exactly\n   1/3 in every session and give the *shared* decoder a comparable target everywhere. A\n   single global threshold would push whole sessions into one class.\n9. **Both inputs and all four outputs are stored time-varying (d, 100)**, per-trial\n   variables being broadcast along time, as the format instructions prefer.\n10. **Session order** follows `bwm_release.csv`, so the conversion is deterministic.\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [x] all clusters/probe ≈ 889 (datapaper)\n- [x] well-isolated clusters/probe ≈ 108 (datapaper)\n- [x] raw trials/session: mean ≈ 645, median ≈ 602, range 401–1525 (datapaper)\n- [x] fraction correct ≈ 0.814 (datapaper)\n- [x] 459 eids / 699 pids / 139 subjects in the freeze file (datapaper)\n- [x] number of retained sessions in the ballpark of the method paper's 433\n- [x] number of Beryl regions in the ballpark of the method paper's 270\n- [x] total well-isolated grey-matter neurons ≈ the data paper's canonical 62,857\n- [x] `probabilityLeft` only ever 0.2 / 0.5 / 0.8, first block = 90 trials at 0.5\n- [x] population PSTH shows a stimulus-locked transient starting at t = 0\n- [x] wheel speed rises at `firstMovement_times` when trials are sorted by reaction time\n- [x] tertile classes each hold ≈1/3 of timepoints\n- [x] element-wise re-derivation of neural/input/output from the raw data (Step 10)\n\n---\n\n## Step 6: Script Development\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`/app/convert_data.py`; runs as\n`python -u /app/convert_data.py <out.pkl> [--full|--sample] [--show-processing] [--n-workers N]`.\n\nStructure:\n- `get_one()` / `get_brain_regions()` — per-process singletons.\n- `load_session_spikes` — brainbox `SpikeSortingLoader` per probe + reference `merge_probes`.\n- `select_neurons` — `label >= 1` and Beryl ∉ {root, void}.\n- `bin_spiking_data_fast` — vectorised replacement for the reference\n  `bin_spiking_data`/`get_spike_data_per_interval`, bin-for-bin identical.\n- `neural_data_available` — ephys-coverage mask.\n- `load_dynamic_behaviour` — reference `load_target_behavior` logic (wheel speed, whisker ME).\n- `bin_behaviour_per_trial` — faithful re-implementation of `get_behavior_per_interval`.\n- `discretize_tertiles`, `trial_number_in_block`.\n- `convert_session` — the per-session pipeline; list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\\n\\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\\n\\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'metadata': {\\n        'task_description': str, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        ...\\n    }\\n}\\n```\\n\\n### Key Format Requirements\\n\\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \\n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\\n\\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \\n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \\n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\\n\\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\\n\\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \\n\\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\\n\\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \\n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \\n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\\n\\n## Python environment\\n\\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\\n\\n## Decoder Reference\\n\\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\\n- Optional arguments:\\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\\n\\n### Purpose\\n\\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\\n1. Perform all of the following checks:\\n\\n**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\\n- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\\n- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \\n- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \\n\\n**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to papers**\\n- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference papers\\n- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the papers's accuracy for each variable\\n- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \\n- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \\n\\n**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\\n- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \\n\\n**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\\n1. Verify the output values are correct by loading raw data and checking 3 specific trials\\n2. Check temporal alignment — plot neural + output for a single trial to verify they're synchronized\\n3. Check whether the output has enough variation (not 99% one class)\\n4. Check that filtering steps for neural activity streams are followed. \\n5. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and papers. \\n\\n**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\\n1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\\n2. Re-run the affected conversion and validation steps\\n3. Re-run ALL checks in this step (not just the one that failed)\\n4. Document each iteration: what was found, what was fixed, what the re-check showed\\n\\n**Report all checks and results** to `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md` to convince the user that the conversion and decoding has been done correctly. \\n\\n**Done when**: You have documented your review findings and all issues are resolved in CONVERSION_NOTES.md under \\\"Step 12\\\".\\n\\n---\\n\\n### Step 13: Documentation and Cleanup\\n\\n**Goal**: Finalize documentation and organize files.\\n\\n**Actions**:\\n- Ensure CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete with all:\\n  - Key decisions and rationale\\n  - Checks for correctness of the conversion\\n  - Validation results and tables\\n  - Any issues found and how they were resolved\\n- Create a user-facing `/app/README.md` summarizing:\\n  - Dataset description\\n  - How to load and use the converted data\\n  - Output format specification\\n  - Key statistics\\n- Move analysis/investigation scripts to a `/app/cache/` folder\\n- Create `/app/cache/README_CACHE.md` documenting cached files\\n\\n**Done when**: README.md exists, CONVERSION_NOTES.md is complete, and directory is clean.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## CONVERSION_NOTES.md Template\\n\\n**Create this file IMMEDIATELY in Step 0. Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allowing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior) about stimulus location. Additionally, wheel speed and whisker motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker motion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference between adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored between nose tip and eye. Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time-varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections “data processing” and “hyperparameter selection” for details.\\n8\\t\\n9\\tData processing\\n10\\t\\n11\\tIBL trial-aligned dataset\\n12\\t\\n13\\tFor choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study,27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5,77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion energy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session.\\n14\\t\\n15\\tIBL trial-unaligned dataset\\n16\\t\\n17\\tWe focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials, capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials.\\n18\\t\\n19\\tFrom \\\"A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour\\\"\\n20\\t\\n21\\tWe trained 139 mice (94 male and 45 female) on the International Brain Laboratory (IBL) decision-making task (Fig. 1a,b). On each trial, a visual stimulus appeared to the left or right on a screen, and the mouse had to move it to the centre by turning a wheel with its front paws within 60 s (Fig. 1c). After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. The next trial began after a delay, followed by a quiescence period during which the mice had to hold the wheel still.\\n22\\t\\n23\\tRecordings\\n24\\t\\n25\\tIn these mice, we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes (see an example of one recording of three trials in Fig. 1i), following a grid that covered the left hemisphere of the forebrain and midbrain, which typically represent stimuli or actions on the contralateral side, and the right hemisphere of the cerebellum and hindbrain, which typically represent the ipsilateral side (Fig. 2a). Recordings were collected by 12 laboratories in Europe and the USA, with most recordings using 2 simultaneous probe insertions. To ensure reproducibility, one brain location was targeted in every mouse in every laboratory, as described elsewhere25. Only sessions with at least 400 trials were retained for further analyses. Data were uploaded to a central server, preprocessed and shared through a standardized interface. To perform spike sorting on the recordings, we used a version of Kilosort with custom additions. This process produced 621,733 units (including multineuron activity), averaging 889 per probe. To separate individual neurons from clusters of multineuron activity, we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.\\n26\\t\\n27\\tMethods\\n28\\t\\n29\\tn brief, at the beginning of each trial, the mouse was required to not move the wheel for a quiescence period of 400–700 ms. After the quiescence period, a visual stimulus (Gabor patch) appeared on either the left or right (±35° azimuth) of the screen, with a contrast randomly sampled from a predefined set (100, 25, 12.5, 6 or 0%). A 100-ms tone (5-kHz sine wave) was played at stimulus onset. Mice had 60 s to move the wheel and make a response. Stimuli were yoked to the rotation of the response wheel, such that a 1-mm movement of the wheel moved the stimulus by 4 visual degrees. A response was registered if the centre of the stimulus crossed the  ±35° azimuth line from its original position. If the mouse correctly moved the stimulus 35° to the centre of the screen, it immediately received a 3-μl reward; if it incorrectly moved the stimulus 35° away from the centre, it received a time out. If the mouse responded incorrectly or failed to reach either threshold within the 60-s window, a white-noise burst was played for 500 ms and the inter-trial interval was between 1 and 1.5 s. In trials for which the visual stimulus contrast was set to 0%, the mouse had to respond as for any other trial by turning the wheel in the correct direction (assigned according to the statistics of the prevailing block) to receive a reward, but the mouse was not able to perceive whether the stimulus was presented on the left or right side of the screen. The mouse also received feedback (noise burst or reward) on 0% contrast trials.\\n30\\t\\n31\\tEach session started with 90 trials in which the probability of a visual stimulus appearing on the left or right side was equal. Specifically, the 100%, 25%, 12.5% and 6% contrast trials were each presented 10 times on each side, and the 0% contrast was presented 10 times in total (that is, the ratio of the 100, 25, 12.5, 6 and 0% contrasts were set at 2, 2, 2, 2 and 1, respectively). The side (and thus correct movement) for the 0% contrast trials was chosen randomly between the right and left with equal probability. This initial block of 90 trials is referred to as the unbiased block (50:50).\\n32\\t\\n33\\tAfter the unbiased block, trials were presented in biased blocks: in right-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 80% of the trials, whereas in left-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 20% of the trials. The ratio of the contrasts remained as above (2:2:2:2:1). Whether the first biased block in a session was left or right was randomly chosen, and blocks were then alternated. The length of a block was drawn from an exponential distribution with scale parameter of 60 trials, but truncated to lie between 20 and 100 trials.\\n34\\t\\n35\\tThe automated shaping protocol for training involved two collections of sessions. In the first session, the animals started performing a version of the task without biased blocks and were then progressively introduced to harder stimuli with weaker contrasts as they became progressively more competent. They also experienced a debiasing protocol, which was intended to dissuade them from persisting with just one of the choices. Once they were performing sufficiently well on all non-zero contrasts, they were faced with the biased blocks. When, in turn, performance on those was adequate (including on 0% contrast trials, which are informed by the block), they graduated to recording. Supplementary Figure 8a shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the first and second collections (these were not correlated). Supplementary Figure 8b shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the second collection and the performance during the recording sessions. The whisker pad area was empirically defined using a rectangular bounding box anchored between the nose tip and the eye, both found using DeepLabCut106 (DLC; see more below). This metric quantifies motion in the whisker pad area and has a temporal resolution of the respective camera.\\n61\\t\\n62\\tWe also performed markerless pose estimation of body parts using DLC31, which is used in a fully automated pipeline in IBL (v.2.1) to track various body parts such as the paws, nose, tongue and pupil (Fig. 1d). Furthermore, we developed several quality-control metrics for the DLC traces105.\\n63\\t\\n64\\tOverview of decoding\\n65\\t\\n66\\tWe performed a decoding analysis to measure how much information the activity of populations of neurons contained about task variables such as stimulus side and choice. To do this we, used cross-validated, maximum-likelihood regression with L1 regularization (to zero out the contribution from noisy neurons). The neural regressors were defined by binning the spike counts from each neuron in each session in a given region in a specific time window on each trial. The duration of the time window, the number of bins in that time window (that is, the bin size) and the trial event to which it was aligned depended on the variable that is the target of our regression (Supplementary Table 2). These factors are discussed further below and include a variety of behavioural and task variables: stimulus side, choice, feedback and wheel speed and velocity. Although a session may have included multiple probe insertions, we did not perform decoding on these probes separately because they are not independent. Instead, neurons in the same session and region were combined across probes for our decoding analysis. Decoding was cross-validated and compared with a null distribution to test for significance. A given region may have been recorded on multiple sessions; therefore, in the main figures (Figs. 4–7) the region P value was defined by combining session P values using Fisher’s combined probability test, and the region effect size was defined by subtracting the median of the null distribution from the decoding score and reporting the median of the resulting values across sessions. The P values for all regions were then subjected to FDR correction for multiple comparisons at q = 0.01.\\n67\\t\\n68\\tDecoding target variables\\n69\\t\\n70\\tStimulus side, choice and feedback were treated as binary target variables for logistic regression. For stimulus side, trials that had zero contrast were excluded. We used the LogisticRegression module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 20,000 maximum iterations, “l1” penalty, “liblinear” solver and “fit_intercept” set to True. We balanced decoder classes by weighting samples by the inverse of the class frequency, 1/(2Pi,class). Decoding performance was evaluated using the balanced accuracy of classification, which is the average of the recall probabilities for the two classes. Supplementary Figure 9 shows histograms of the regression coefficients for all the variables.\\n71\\t\\n72\\tWheel values (speed and velocity) change over the course of a trial, unlike the previous decoding targets, and we therefore had to treat these target variables differently. We averaged wheel values in nonoverlapping 20-ms bins, starting 200 ms before first wheel-movement time and ending at 1,000 ms after first wheel-movement time. Spike counts were similarly binned. The target value for a given bin (ending at time t) was decoded from spikes in a preceding (causal) window spanning W bins (ending at times t, …, t-W). Therefore, if decoding from n neurons, there were (W + 1)n predictors of the target variable in a given bin. In practice, we used W = 10. To decode these continuous-valued targets, we performed linear regression using the Lasso module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 1,000 maximum iterations and “fit_intercept” set to True. Whisker motion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference between adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored between nose tip and eye. Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time-varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections “data processing” and “hyperparameter selection” for details.\\\\n\\\\nData processing\\\\n\\\\nIBL trial-aligned dataset\\\\n\\\\nFor choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study,27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5,77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion energy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session.\\\\n\\\\nIBL trial-unaligned dataset\\\\n\\\\nWe focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials, capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials.\\\\n\\\\nFrom \\\\\\\"A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nWe trained 139 mice (94 male and 45 female) on the International Brain Laboratory (IBL) decision-making task (Fig. 1a,b). On each trial, a visual stimulus appeared to the left or right on a screen, and the mouse had to move it to the centre by turning a wheel with its front paws within 60 s (Fig. 1c). After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. The next trial began after a delay, followed by a quiescence period during which the mice had to hold the wheel still.\\\\n\\\\nRecordings\\\\n\\\\nIn these mice, we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes (see an example of one recording of three trials in Fig. 1i), following a grid that covered the left hemisphere of the forebrain and midbrain, which typically represent stimuli or actions on the contralateral side, and the right hemisphere of the cerebellum and hindbrain, which typically represent the ipsilateral side (Fig. 2a). Recordings were collected by 12 laboratories in Europe and the USA, with most recordings using 2 simultaneous probe insertions. To ensure reproducibility, one brain location was targeted in every mouse in every laboratory, as described elsewhere25. Only sessions with at least 400 trials were retained for further analyses. Data were uploaded to a central server, preprocessed and shared through a standardized interface. To perform spike sorting on the recordings, we used a version of Kilosort with custom additions. This process produced 621,733 units (including multineuron activity), averaging 889 per probe. To separate individual neurons from clusters of multineuron activity, we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.\\\\n\\\\nMethods\\\\n\\\\nn brief, at the beginning of each trial, the mouse was required to not move the wheel for a quiescence period of 400–700 ms. After the quiescence period, a visual stimulus (Gabor patch) appeared on either the left or right (±35° azimuth) of the screen, with a contrast randomly sampled from a predefined set (100, 25, 12.5, 6 or 0%). A 100-ms tone (5-kHz sine wave) was played at stimulus onset. Mice had 60 s to move the wheel and make a response. Stimuli were yoked to the rotation of the response wheel, such that a 1-mm movement of the wheel moved the stimulus by 4 visual degrees. A response was registered if the centre of the stimulus crossed the  ±35° azimuth line from its original position. If the mouse correctly moved the stimulus 35° to the centre of the screen, it immediately received a 3-μl reward; if it incorrectly moved the stimulus 35° away from the centre, it received a time out. If the mouse responded incorrectly or failed to reach either threshold within the 60-s window, a white-noise burst was played for 500 ms and the inter-trial interval was between 1 and 1.5 s. In trials for which the visual stimulus contrast was set to 0%, the mouse had to respond as for any other trial by turning the wheel in the correct direction (assigned according to the statistics of the prevailing block) to receive a reward, but the mouse was not able to perceive whether the stimulus was presented on the left or right side of the screen. The mouse also received feedback (noise burst or reward) on 0% contrast trials.\\\\n\\\\nEach session started with 90 trials in which the probability of a visual stimulus appearing on the left or right side was equal. Specifically, the 100%, 25%, 12.5% and 6% contrast trials were each presented 10 times on each side, and the 0% contrast was presented 10 times in total (that is, the ratio of the 100, 25, 12.5, 6 and 0% contrasts were set at 2, 2, 2, 2 and 1, respectively). The side (and thus correct movement) for the 0% contrast trials was chosen randomly between the right and left with equal probability. This initial block of 90 trials is referred to as the unbiased block (50:50).\\\\n\\\\nAfter the unbiased block, trials were presented in biased blocks: in right-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 80% of the trials, whereas in left-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 20% of the trials. The ratio of the contrasts remained as above (2:2:2:2:1). Whether the first biased block in a session was left or right was randomly chosen, and blocks were then alternated. The length of a block was drawn from an exponential distribution with scale parameter of 60 trials, but truncated to lie between 20 and 100 trials.\\\\n\\\\nThe automated shaping protocol for training involved two collections of sessions. In the first session, the animals started performing a version of the task without biased blocks and were then progressively introduced to harder stimuli with weaker contrasts as they became progressively more competent. They also experienced a debiasing protocol, which was intended to dissuade them from persisting with just one of the choices. Once they were performing sufficiently well on all non-zero contrasts, they were faced with the biased blocks. When, in turn, performance on those was adequate (including on 0% contrast trials, which are informed by the block), they graduated to recording. Supplementary Figure 8a shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the first and second collections (these were not correlated). Supplementary Figure 8b shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the second collection and the performance during the recording sessions. These were also not correlated.\\\\n\\\\nInclusion criteria\\\\n\\\\nWe applied a set of inclusion criteria to sessions, probes and neurons to ensure data quality. Supplementary Table 1 lists the consequences of these criteria for the number of sessions and probes that passed the criteria.\\\\nSessions and insertions\\\\n\\\\nEach Neuropixels insertion was repeated in at least two laboratories, with reproducibility of outcomes across laboratories verified with extensive analyses that we have previously reported25.\\\\n\\\\nSessions were included in the data release if the mice performed at least 250 trials, with a performance of at least 90% correct on 100% contrast trials for both left and right blocks, and, to be able to analyse the feedback variable, if there were at least 3 trials with incorrect choices (after applying the trial exclusions below). Furthermore, sessions were included in the release only if they reached threshold on a collection of hardware tests (definitions are available from GiHub (https://int-brain-lab.github.io/iblenv/_autosummary/ibllib.qc.task_metrics.html)).\\\\n\\\\nInsertions were excluded if the neural data failed the whole recording per visually assessed criteria of the ‘Recording Inclusion metrics and Guidelines for Optimal Reproducibility’ (RIGOR) from ref. 25, by presenting major artefacts (see examples in ref. 28) or if the probe tract could not be recovered during the histology procedure. Furthermore, only insertions for which alignments had been resolved (see appendix 6 of ref. 25 for definitions) were used in this study.\\\\n\\\\nAfter applying these criteria, a total of 459 sessions, 699 insertions and 621,733 neurons remained, constituting the publicly released dataset.\\\\nTrials\\\\n\\\\nFor the analyses presented here, trials were excluded if one of the following trial events could not be detected: choice, probabilityLeft, feebackType, feeback times, stimON times and firstMovement times. Trials were further excluded if the time between stimulus onset and the first movement of the wheel (the first wheel-movement time) were outside the range of 0.08–2.00 s.\\\\nNeurons and brain regions\\\\n\\\\nNeurons generated by the spike-sorting pipeline were excluded from the analyses presented here if they failed one of the three criteria described in ref. 28 (the single unit computed metrics of RIGOR25): amplitude > 50 μV; noise cut-off < 20 μV; and refractory period violation. Neurons that passed these criteria were termed well-isolated neurons (or often just ‘neurons’) in this study. Out of the 621,733 units collected, 75,708 were considered well-isolated neurons. Final analyses were additionally restricted to regions that were designated grey matter in the adult mouse Allen Common Coordinate framework6, contained at least five well-isolated neurons per session and were recorded from in at least two such sessions.\\\\n\\\\nVideo analysis\\\\n\\\\nWe briefly describe the video analysis pipeline (full details can be found in ref. 105). The recording rigs contained three cameras: one called ‘left’ at full resolution (1,280 × 1,024) and 60 Hz, filming the mouse from one side; one called ‘right’, filming the mouse symmetrically from the other side at half resolution (640 × 512) and 150 Hz; and one called ‘body’ at half resolution and 30 Hz, filming the body of the mouse from above. We developed several quality-control metrics to detect raw video issues such as poor illumination (as infrared light bulbs broke) or accidental misplacement of the cameras105.\\\\n\\\\nWe computed the motion energy (the mean across pixels of the absolute value of the difference between adjacent frames) of the whisker pad areas in the ‘left’ and ‘right’ videos (Fig. 1d). The whisker pad area was empirically defined using a rectangular bounding box anchored between the nose tip and the eye, both found using DeepLabCut106 (DLC; see more below). This metric quantifies motion in the whisker pad area and has a temporal resolution of the respective camera.\\\\n\\\\nWe also performed markerless pose estimation of body parts using DLC31, which is used in a fully automated pipeline in IBL (v.2.1) to track various body parts such as the paws, nose, tongue and pupil (Fig. 1d). In all analyses using DLC estimates, we excluded predictions with likelihood < 0.9. Furthermore, we developed several quality-control metrics for the DLC traces105.\\\\n\\\\nOverview of decoding\\\\n\\\\nWe performed a decoding analysis to measure how much information the activity of populations of neurons contained about task variables such as stimulus side and choice. To do this we, used cross-validated, maximum-likelihood regression with L1 regularization (to zero out the contribution from noisy neurons). The neural regressors were defined by binning the spike counts from each neuron in each session in a given region in a specific time window on each trial. The duration of the time window, the number of bins in that time window (that is, the bin size) and the trial event to which it was aligned depended on the variable that is the target of our regression (Supplementary Table 2). These factors are discussed further below and include a variety of behavioural and task variables: stimulus side, choice, feedback and wheel speed and velocity. Although a session may have included multiple probe insertions, we did not perform decoding on these probes separately because they are not independent. Instead, neurons in the same session and region were combined across probes for our decoding analysis. Decoding was cross-validated and compared with a null distribution to test for significance. A given region may have been recorded on multiple sessions; therefore, in the main figures (Figs. 4–7) the region P value was defined by combining session P values using Fisher’s combined probability test, and the region effect size was defined by subtracting the median of the null distribution from the decoding score and reporting the median of the resulting values across sessions. The P values for all regions were then subjected to FDR correction for multiple comparisons at q = 0.01.\\\\n\\\\nDecoding target variables\\\\n\\\\nStimulus side, choice and feedback were treated as binary target variables for logistic regression. For stimulus side, trials that had zero contrast were excluded. We used the LogisticRegression module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 20,000 maximum iterations, “l1” penalty, “liblinear” solver and “fit_intercept” set to True. We balanced decoder classes by weighting samples by the inverse of the class frequency, 1/(2Pi,class). Decoding performance was evaluated using the balanced accuracy of classification, which is the average of the recall probabilities for the two classes. Supplementary Figure 9 shows histograms of the regression coefficients for all the variables.\\\\n\\\\nWheel values (speed and velocity) change over the course of a trial, unlike the previous decoding targets, and we therefore had to treat these target variables differently. We averaged wheel values in nonoverlapping 20-ms bins, starting 200 ms before first wheel-movement time and ending at 1,000 ms after first wheel-movement time. Spike counts were similarly binned. The target value for a given bin (ending at time t) was decoded from spikes in a preceding (causal) window spanning W bins (ending at times t, …, t-W). Therefore, if decoding from n neurons, there were (W + 1)n predictors of the target variable in a given bin. In practice, we used W = 10. To decode these continuous-valued targets, we performed linear regression using the Lasso module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 1,000 maximum iterations and “fit_intercept” set to True. Decoding performance was evaluated using the R2 metric.\\\\n\\\", \\\"numLines\\\": 73, \\\"startLine\\\": 1, \\\"totalLines\\\": 73}}\",\n/logs/agent/trajectory.json:1264:                    \"content\": \"From \\\"Exploiting correlations across trials and behavioral sessions to improve neural decoding\\\"\\n\\nOur goal is to decode behavior y \\\\in R^P from spike-sorted, temporally binned spike counts.
